article_title: Fraction Face-Off!
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2020, March). Fraction Face-Off!. Retrieved from https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Four-activity lesson structure combining explicit instruction, fluency games, and individual practice
description: Each Fraction Face-Off! lesson follows a fixed four-activity structure: "a warm-up word problem, group work during which the teacher demonstrates fraction concepts using explicit instruction, a speed game to build fluency, and a worksheet activity that students complete individually to check their understanding of the fraction concepts." The program pairs frequent fluency practice using speed tests or flashcards with conceptual practice requiring students to explain their reasoning about fractions to the group, plus ongoing assessment through daily worksheets and a cumulative review.
requirements: Up to a week of training for teachers before delivering content, with 1-hour follow-up meetings every other week
constraints: Lessons varied in length between 30 and 35 minutes in the study, and in years 2 through 5 only 25 minutes of each session were the same across the two intervention conditions
target_learners: fourth-grade students who need assistance solving fraction problems
examples: In year 1, each lesson included introduction of concepts or skills (8-12 minutes), group work (8-12 minutes), the speed game (1 minute), and individual work (8 minutes)
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2020, March). Fraction Face-Off!. Retrieved from https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/702

article_title: Fraction Face-Off!
citation: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2020, March). Fraction Face-Off!. Retrieved from https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Deliver supplemental fraction tutoring in small groups three times weekly for 12 weeks
description: The developer recommends "students use Fraction Face-Off! three times a week for 12 weeks for about 30 minutes per session." This dosage was the schedule under which the program's positive effects were demonstrated: in the contributing study, the intervention was delivered three times per week for 12 weeks between September/October and early February, in small groups at a three-to-one ratio, typically during class time or a pull-out time to supplement the math curriculum.
requirements: Schools must provide classroom space if the intervention is not implemented in the student's regular classroom, and make copies of materials and manipulatives for all participating students
constraints: The recommended dosage is three 30- to 35-minute lessons per week; the study delivered sessions during one of three instructional periods of typically 50, 20, or 45 minutes
target_learners: fourth-grade students who have demonstrated difficulty in mathematics
examples: Within each study class, the intervention was delivered by one teacher to small groups (three-to-one ratio) three times per week for 12 weeks, with each teacher responsible for two to four groups

article_title: The Network for College Success
citation: Pitcher, M. A., Duncan, S. J., Nagaoka, J., Moeller, E., Dickerson, L., & Beechum, N. O. (2016). The Network for College Success: A Capacity-Building Model for School Improvement. University of Chicago. https://ncs.uchicago.edu
title: Freshman On-Track indicator and Individual School Report
description: The Freshman On-Track indicator is a research-based early-warning metric: a student is On-Track if he or she earns at least five full-year course credits and no more than one semester F in a core course in ninth grade. Its simplicity makes it easy to calculate with school-generated data. CPS began providing real-time early-warning data reports in 2008, and the Freshman On Track Individual School Report (ISR) was developed to provide customized data so school leaders can analyze trends and set measurable goals. The paper also notes an accompanying Freshman On-Track Toolkit organized around four components including Developing Capacity & Leadership and Applying Research & Data.

constraints: The paper notes concerns arose that On-Track improvements might not represent true changes in performance, which a subsequent Consortium study addressed
target_learners: Ninth-grade students in urban high schools, supported by principals, counselors, and grade-level teacher teams
target_learning_goals: Increasing freshman course passing and On-Track status as a foundation for high school graduation
examples: CPS adapted the year-end metric for point-in-time monitoring throughout the year to flag students in need of interventions

article_title: The friction paradox: generative AI and the educational value of difficulty in education abroad
citation: Gupta, K. (2026). The friction paradox: generative AI and the educational value of difficulty in education abroad. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10609387/v1
title: The friction paradox: generative AI can widen access to education abroad while weakening a principal learning mechanism
description: The friction paradox holds that the same generative AI system can remove an exclusionary language barrier in one context and eliminate a valuable communicative encounter in another. The article states that "generative AI can simultaneously make education abroad more inclusive and weaken one of its principal learning mechanisms". It extends desirable-difficulties and productive-failure arguments to relational difficulty within cross-cultural encounters, where difficulty is relational, interpretively open, and avoidance is socially invisible.
requirements: Institutional policy must distinguish barriers that exclude students from encounters that develop them, since removing both indiscriminately may leave education abroad more convenient but less educational
constraints: The framework is conceptual and untested; the article states the propositions in Section 6 may not survive examination
target_learners: students in cross-border education-abroad programmes, both short-term/semester and full-degree mobility
examples: The article contrasts translating an emergency medical instruction, which protects access, with translating every informal conversation, which may reduce language development and relationship formation
key_sources: Gupta, K. (2026). The friction paradox: generative AI and the educational value of difficulty in education abroad. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10609387/v1

article_title: The friction paradox: generative AI and the educational value of difficulty in education abroad
citation: Gupta, K. (2026). The friction paradox: generative AI and the educational value of difficulty in education abroad. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10609387/v1
title: Two-dimensional taxonomy of friction: harmful and productive friction by educational function, synthetic friction by technological origin
description: The taxonomy separates friction classified by educational function from friction generated by the technology itself. "Harmful friction and productive friction classify difficulty by educational function: whether it excludes the student from participation or creates conditions in which learning may occur." Synthetic friction classifies difficulty by technological origin — difficulty created or intensified by AI inaccuracy, cultural reduction, false confidence or inappropriate substitution — and its educational function remains open. The dimensions intersect rather than form three positions on one scale.
requirements: Synthetic friction should be made visible and contestable rather than simply eliminated, because its educational function depends on whether it is detected and examined
constraints: The taxonomy rejects friction romanticism, in which difficulty is presumed to build resilience and support is denied, and friction elimination, in which every uncertainty is treated as an inefficiency
target_learning_goals: distinguishing exclusionary barriers from developmentally productive difficulty
examples: Table 1 lists examples: harmful friction includes inability to communicate a medical condition; productive friction includes attempting a host-language interaction; synthetic friction includes incorrect translation and stereotyped cultural explanation
key_sources: Gupta, K. (2026). The friction paradox: generative AI and the educational value of difficulty in education abroad. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10609387/v1

article_title: The friction paradox: generative AI and the educational value of difficulty in education abroad
citation: Gupta, K. (2026). The friction paradox: generative AI and the educational value of difficulty in education abroad. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10609387/v1
title: Friction-conversion principle: reduce harmful friction, convert manageable difficulty, preserve interpretive role, expose synthetic friction
description: The article proposes that "responsible AI in education abroad should reduce harmful friction, convert manageable difficulty into supported participation, preserve the student's interpretive role in productive encounters, and make synthetic friction visible and contestable". Friction conversion differs from friction removal: the objective is to change the conditions under which difficulty is encountered rather than to eliminate the difficulty. The principle places educational purpose before technological efficiency.
requirements: Programmes must be able to classify friction by type before deciding whether to remove, convert or expose it
constraints: Productive friction should not be maximised indiscriminately but preserved in a form students can engage with safely and reflectively
examples: Instead of writing the student's complaint to a landlord, AI helps identify the issue, explains possible tones, teaches relevant phrases and asks the student to select and personalise the message

citation: Dai (2026). Rethinking AI-assisted writing instruction: feedback literacy scripts, calibration training, and student writing development. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1829268
title: FRAC Feedback Literacy Script (Filter–Reason–Act–Check)
description: FRAC is a four-step feedback literacy script that guides students' processing of external AI feedback: "Filter, identifying the type of problem addressed by the feedback; Reason, judging whether the feedback was valid and relevant to the current task", then Act (implementing adopted feedback as a specific revision) and Check (reviewing whether the revision achieved the intended result). Training lasted approximately 15 to 25 minutes before T1 with brief reviews before T1 and T2; students recorded decision sheets at T1 and T2 as process data, with return rates exceeding 90% per round.

target_learning_goals: critical evaluation and effective uptake of AI-generated writing feedback
examples: FRAC group and combined group students completed decision sheets at T1 and T2 recording how they processed AI feedback; implementation was verified through submission rates, completeness checks, and classroom observations

article_title: StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators
citation: Ke Yang, Chenglong Wang, Michel Galley, Chandan Singh, Jeevana Priya Inala, ChengXiang Zhai, Jianfeng Gao. (2026). StudentSim: Training LLM-based Student Simulators. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01591
title: The F/R decomposition: student simulators as jointly faithful and guidance-responsive proxies for tutor optimization
description: The article formalizes per-student student simulation as a measurable target with two properties. First, "behavioral fidelity: how well the simulator reproduces a student's own response to a problem, including that student's characteristic mistakes and strengths". Second, "guidance responsiveness", how readily the simulator updates its response in the direction tutor guidance steers. The framework is motivated by educational measurement's two targets — independent production and progress with support, the zone of proximal development that dynamic assessment operationalizes — and turns student simulation into an optimizable objective for AI tutor training.
requirements: A useful simulator must satisfy both properties together; the high-F, high-R corner is the target, since F and R measure separable capabilities.
constraints: The authors note F and R capture a student's state and its one-step update under guidance, not fuller learning dynamics such as acquisition, retention, and forgetting across many interactions.
target_learners: individual real learners in chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics
target_learning_goals: reproducing individual student responses and their revision under tutor guidance
examples: The framework scores every method on the same held-out per-student records, e.g. chess fidelity as move-prediction accuracy and responsiveness as corrected-move rate.

article_title: Against frictionless AI
citation: Emily Zohar, Paul Bloom & Michael Inzlicht. (2026). Against frictionless AI. Communications Psychology 4:39. https://doi.org/10.1038/s44271-026-00402-1
title: Friction as a construct: difficulty during goal pursuit that enhances learning, meaning, and motivation
description: The article defines friction as "the experience of difficulty during goal pursuit, often accompanied by negative feelings like frustration and corrective feedback" and argues it "enhances learning, generates meaning and pleasure, and makes us better people." It organizes the comment around applying this construct to intellectual work and social relationships, warning that frictionless AI strips away beneficial friction along with excess friction.
requirements: Friction must be moderate rather than excessive to produce benefits
constraints: The authors state friction's benefits are not unlimited; excessive friction overwhelms
target_learners: AI users in academic and everyday settings
examples: The article contrasts a hiker reaching a summit through sustained effort with someone taking a chairlift to the same destination

citation: Black, P., & Wiliam, D. (2009). Developing the theory of formative assessment. Educ Asse Eval Acc, 21, 5–31. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11092-008-9068-5
title: Use a theoretical framework of formative assessment to open up new ways of helping teachers implement formative practices more effectively.
description: The article recommends that developing theory for formative assessment should serve practice directly: a sound framework should both guide research and support teacher implementation. The abstract states the framework "should indicate potentially fruitful lines for further enquiry, whilst at the same time opening up new ways of helping teachers to implement formative practices more effectively." The principle is that theoretical clarification of formative assessment is a route to more effective professional support for teachers, not merely an academic exercise.
requirements: A coherent framework delimiting formative assessment within pedagogy, so that implementation support can be grounded in it.
constraints: The article states this as an intended payoff of the framework; it does not report tested implementation outcomes in the accessible text.
target_learning_goals: More effective classroom implementation of formative assessment practices
examples: The article frames its framework as serving both further enquiry and teacher implementation support.

article_title: The role of feedback in adult second language acquisition: Error correction and morphological generalizations
citation: Susanne Carroll, Merrill Swain, and Yves Roberge. (1992). The role of feedback in adult second language acquisition: Error correction and morphological generalizations. Applied Psycholinguistics, Volume 13, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0142716400005555
title: Experimental French suffixation feedback-training task with feedback and guessing sessions
description: The study's instrument was an individual training task on two rules of French suffixation administered to 79 adult native speakers of English with intermediate (39) and advanced (40) proficiency in French. In the article's words, "Experimental subjects received correction if they gave erroneous responses to stimuli in a “feedback” session." Afterward all subjects guessed responses to novel stimuli and were retested twice on the feedback items, while comparison subjects "dealt with the same stimuli but were never corrected."
requirements: Subjects must be individually trained on the two suffixation rules before the feedback session
constraints: The task was administered in an experimental setting with adult intermediate and advanced French learners, not in ordinary classroom instruction
target_learners: adult intermediate and advanced learners of French
target_learning_goals: learning morphological generalizations of French suffixation, including absolute exceptions
examples: Experimental subjects were corrected for erroneous responses during the feedback session; comparison subjects handled the same stimuli without correction

article_title: Audience effects on the neural correlates of relational reasoning in adolescence
citation: Dumontheil Iroise, Wolf Laura K., Blakemore Sarah-Jayne. (2016). Audience effects on the neural correlates of relational reasoning in adolescence. Neuropsychologia. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuropsychologia.2016.05.001
title: Fronto-parietal relational-integration network
description: The article describes relational reasoning as engaging "a fronto-parietal network including the inferior parietal cortex, pre-supplementary motor area, dorsolateral and rostrolateral prefrontal cortices", with the rostrolateral prefrontal cortex specifically associated with relational integration. In the study, this network was functionally defined by the Relational>Control contrast and served as the region-of-interest for testing audience and age modulation. It provides the neural framework within which the peer audience effects were interpreted.
requirements: Defined empirically via the Relational>Control contrast at voxel-level p<0.001 uncorrected and cluster-level pFWE<0.05
constraints: The study examined female participants only, aged 14–16 and 23–28 years
target_learning_goals: fluid reasoning associated with academic achievement
examples: The contrast revealed activations in preSMA, bilateral inferior and superior parietal lobules, bilateral occipital cortex and bilateral frontal clusters extending into the RLPFC

article_title: Self-regulation in the pre-adolescent brain
citation: Pas P., Hulshoff Pol H.E., Raemaekers M., Vink M. (2021). Self-regulation in the pre-adolescent brain. Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2021.101012
title: Frontal control over subcortical regions as the developmental basis of proactive inhibitory control
description: The article works within a framework in which self-regulation develops through the integration of low-level executive functions such as reactive inhibition into higher-level proactive control, which "has been theorized to depend upon the establishment of frontal control over the rest of the brain, in particular subcortical regions". On this account, the shift from reactive to proactive inhibition strategies is linked to increased frontal activation and increased functional coupling between frontal and subcortical regions. The study tests this framework in pre-adolescent children by relating questionnaire-based self-regulation to frontal activation and cortico-subcortical coupling during a stop-signal anticipation task.
requirements: Measurement of both reactive and proactive inhibition with concurrent fMRI to index frontal activation and functional coupling
constraints: The article notes its cross-sectional data does not provide a definitive answer to how self-regulation increases relate to neural changes
examples: The study related EATQ-R self-regulation scores to right mid frontal cortex activation and striatal-motor coupling in 640 children performing the Stop-Signal Anticipation Task

article_title: It is not either or: An initial investigation into combining collaborative and individual learning using an ITS
citation: Olsen, J. K., Rummel, N., & Aleven, V. (2019). It is not either or: An initial investigation into combining collaborative and individual learning using an ITS. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 14, 353-381. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-019-09307-0
title: Intelligent tutoring system for fractions used in individual, collaborative, and combined learning conditions
description: An intelligent tutoring system for fractions served as the core learning environment in this study, deployed with "382 4th and 5th grade students" across three conditions: a combined condition and "individual or collaborative-only learning conditions." The ITS logged process data on students' hints and errors over time, which the authors analyzed to compare conditions, and the activity supported reported situational interest measures.
requirements: The ITS must support both individual and collaborative use so that conditions can be compared on the same content.

article_title: Data to decision-making: how elementary students use their Community and Citizen Science project to reimagine their school campus
citation: Erin Bridges Bird · Heidi L. Ballard · Margaret Harte. (2023). Data to decision-making: how elementary students use their Community and Citizen Science project to reimagine their school campus. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-022-09612-6
title: Three knowledge types for environmental decision-making: systems, action-related, and effectiveness knowledge
description: The article adopts Frick et al.'s framework of three knowledge types used in environmental decision-making. Systems knowledge is "understanding of the natural states of ecosystems and the processes within them"; action-related knowledge is knowledge needed to address a particular problem, applied for direct or indirect impact; effectiveness knowledge is needed "when there are different ways to act" to evaluate and justify what "effective" means. The article uses this lens to analyze what students knew versus lacked when deciding.
requirements: Deciding what action to take requires more than content knowledge: learners also need action-related and effectiveness knowledge
constraints: The article notes having knowledge about a system still does not provide clear understanding about what action can be taken
examples: Garret had action-related knowledge to indirectly mitigate invasive species by planting more native species, while students in the predator-prey problem space lacked the action-related knowledge to know what to do

article_title: Teachers’ judgment accuracy of students’ monitoring skills: a conceptual and methodological framework and explorative study
citation: van de Pol, J., & Oudman, S. (2024). Teachers' judgment accuracy of students' monitoring skills: a conceptual and methodological framework and explorative study. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09349-8
title: Framework of teachers' judgments of students' monitoring skills with three accuracy measures
description: The article introduces a framework that integrates teachers' judgments of students' performance, teachers' judgments of students' monitoring judgments, and students' actual performance and monitoring judgments. It defines three measures: 'Teachers' judgment accuracy of students' monitoring judgments is captured with three measures' — SMA-TJ (student monitoring accuracy according to teacher judgments), TJASMJ (teacher judgment accuracy of the student's monitoring judgment), and C-SMA-TJ (correctness of student monitoring accuracy according to teacher judgments). The framework 'applies to every classroom situation, regardless of the proportion of optimists/pessimists/realists' and serves both to conceptualize the constructs and as a guideline for operationalizing them, unlike the earlier categoric approach.
requirements: Requires measuring teachers' judgments of student performance (TJSP), teachers' judgments of students' monitoring judgments (TJSMJ), students' monitoring judgments (SMJ), and students' actual performance (SP) to compute the deviation indices
constraints: The article focuses on absolute accuracy and bias measures; it defers discussion of relative accuracy measures to its Discussion section
target_learners: secondary education students whose monitoring skills are judged by their teachers
target_learning_goals: teachers' accurate judgment of students' self-monitoring of reading comprehension performance
examples: A numeric example (Fig. 2) walks through a student scoring 2 points, judging 4, with a teacher judging performance at 5 and the monitoring judgment at 2, yielding SMA-TJ, TJASMJ and C-SMA-TJ values
key_sources: van de Pol, J., & Oudman, S. (2024). Teachers' judgment accuracy of students' monitoring skills: a conceptual and methodological framework and explorative study. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-023-09349-8

citation: Fernando Núñez-Regueiro, Herbert W Marsh, Reinhard Pekrun, Oliver Lüdtke, Jiesi Guo. (2025). The Reciprocal Effects Model is Robust to Alternative Modeling Specifications: A Response to Sorjonen et al., 2025. Educational Psychology Review, 37 (3), pp.79. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10059-7
title: Comparative framework for longitudinal models differing in change processes, temporal structure, and measurement design
description: Beyond responding to the commentary, the authors "present a generalizable framework for comparing longitudinal models that differ in their assumptions about change processes, temporal structure, and measurement design." The framework organizes model comparison around three axes: what change process a model assumes, how it represents temporal structure (e.g., lag0 and lag1 effects), and what measurement design it presumes. It is used in the article to reanalyze the simulated and PALMA data and evaluate the extended REM against alternatives.
requirements: Longitudinal data and candidate models whose assumptions about change processes, temporal structure, and measurement design can be made explicit and compared.
target_learning_goals: Selecting and validating longitudinal models of reciprocal learning-related processes
examples: The framework was applied to reanalyze both the simulated data constructed by Sorjonen et al. and the original PALMA dataset.

article_title: Using Primary Knowledge: an Efficient Way To Motivate Students and Promote the Learning of Formal Reasoning
citation: Florence Lespiau, André Tricot. (2019). Using Primary Knowledge: an Efficient Way To Motivate Students and Promote the Learning of Formal Reasoning. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09482-4
title: Frame practice of formal reasoning in evolutionary-salient primary knowledge contexts to motivate learners
description: The article recommends using primary knowledge contents to facilitate learning of formal logical rules: "Framing formal logical problems in evolutionary salient contexts should increase learners' efficiency, motivation and engagement in learning compared with framing logical problems in secondary knowledge". In practice, formal problems are given concrete, evolutionarily familiar cover stories (food, animals) rather than abstract or school-like content. The authors present this as a cost-efficient way of keeping learners motivated whatever their age or personal characteristics.
requirements: Formal problems must use unknown content to reduce the use of prior knowledge
Primary and secondary versions of the problems must be structurally equivalent
constraints: Benefit demonstrated for syllogism-style formal reasoning tasks with invented content
examples: High school students trained with syllogisms about invented food and animals versus fictitious mathematics and grammar rules; university students received a primary-knowledge priming phase before secondary-knowledge training

article_title: The framework of prior knowledge in online credibility evaluation
citation: Carita Kiili, Ivar Bråten, and Julie Coiro. (2026). The framework of prior knowledge in online credibility evaluation. Educational Psychologist. https://doi.org/10.1080/00461520.2026.2717081
title: The Framework of Prior Knowledge in Online Credibility Evaluation
description: The article proposes a framework in which online credibility evaluation by a motivated, strategic reader draws on five interconnected prior knowledge types. As printed, "the framework consists of four main interacting components: prior knowledge, evaluation strategies, metastrategic knowledge and regulation, and justified integrated understanding." Activated knowledge supports inferences about content, source, and context credibility, and resulting understanding can be integrated into existing knowledge structures to support future evaluations.
requirements: Readers must be motivated and strategic; the framework intentionally focuses on evaluation processes of a motivated and strategic reader rather than heuristic processing
constraints: The framework enjoys preliminary empirical support and is proposed to promote further empirical work investigating its crucial assumptions
The five knowledge types are distinguished for analytical purposes and may be highly intertwined in practice
target_learners: online readers evaluating the credibility of web information
adolescent and adult students in educational settings
target_learning_goals: critical online reading and credibility evaluation of online information

article_title: A consideration of racial/ethnic diversity conceptualization and measurement: Clarifying ambiguities and advancing scholarship
citation: Chan, M.-k., & Benner, A. D. (2023). A Consideration of Racial/Ethnic Diversity Conceptualization and Measurement: Clarifying Ambiguities and Advancing Scholarship. Educational Psychologist (accepted manuscript). https://orcid.org/0000-0001-6451-2417
title: Frequentist-based Representative Diversity (FRD) index: a new measure capturing dual-concept and representative diversity simultaneously
description: The FRD index is a proposed measure that modifies the dissimilarity (segregation) index to "assess the degree of similarity between a target and a reference population", computed as one minus the summed absolute differences between target and reference group proportions. The researcher specifies a target distribution and a reference population "set by the researcher to represent maximum diversity in a given context." The authors state it "can capture two different aspects of diversity, is easy to interpret, and potentially broadens the scope of diversity research." It addresses the absence of tools for representative diversity and limitations of existing dual-concept indices.
requirements: The researcher must specify a target distribution and a reference population representing maximum diversity in the given context
constraints: Proposed in an accepted manuscript; the supplied text does not report empirical validation studies of the index
target_learning_goals: quantifying school racial/ethnic diversity in a way that preserves minority-representation information and compares contexts to reference populations
examples: The article illustrates the formula with a school that is 50% White, 30% Latina/o/x, and 20% Black, comparing its AP Calculus class composition to the school composition

article_title: Supported self-explaining during fraction intervention.
citation: Fuchs, L. S., Malone, A., Schumacher, R. F., Namkung, J., Hamlett, C. L., Jordan, N. C., Siegler, R. S., Gersten, R., & Changas, P. (2016). Supported Self-Explaining during Fraction Intervention. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000073
title: Fraction Face-Off! multi-component fraction intervention
description: Fraction Face-Off! is the multi-component fraction intervention in which both the explaining and word-problem components were embedded. "Sessions occurred 3 times per week for 12 weeks with pairs of children," each 35 minutes, with 28 shared minutes focused on the measurement interpretation: comparing, ordering, placing fractions on number lines, and equivalencies. Instruction was explicit with worked examples, efficient strategies, cumulative review, and a motivation system of checkmarks, fraction dollars, and a weekly Fraction Store.
requirements: Tutor training, manualized materials, fidelity monitoring via audiotapes, and bi-weekly meetings to avoid contamination between conditions
constraints: Focused mainly on the measurement interpretation with a limited range of denominators (2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 10, 12)
target_learners: fourth graders below the 35th percentile in calculations
examples: Number lines reflected 70% of the intervention's emphasis versus 20.87% in control classrooms

article_title: Recent studies in handwriting.
citation: Thompson, M. E. (1911). Recent Studies in Handwriting. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 2, 41-45.
title: Freeman's recommendations: emphasize letter form from the start, postpone strenuous movement drill, and combine sentence and letter methods
description: On the basis of his own and other experiments, Freeman discusses five questions in the teaching of writing. He argues that form, which is fundamental, should be emphasized from the start while strenuous drill in movement may be postponed until the third or fourth grade, that slant writing has a physiological basis for greater ease and rapidity, and that a combination of sentence and letter method is advantageous.
requirements: Further experimentation is recognized as needed throughout the discussion
constraints: Drill in arm movement shows little progress in the first three or four grades, with marked development in grades IV to VI
examples: Freeman suggests taking one component at a time, practicing finger movement at the desk and arm movement at the blackboard, and uniting the two later; a combination of free arm movement, muscular movement, and finger movement is advocated

article_title: A Further Criterion for the Selection of Mental Test Elements.
citation: Chapman, J. Crosby and Dale, A. Barbara. (1921). A Further Criterion for the Selection of Mental Test Elements. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://archive.org/search?query=A+Further+Criterion+for+the+Selection+of+Mental+Test+Elements
title: Test elements intended to measure higher mental processes must be freed from non-essential experience factors
description: Because intelligence is measured through higher complex processes that must reveal themselves in young bright children, the article argues "The test elements which measure the presence or absence of these powers must be freed from non-essential experience factors." Otherwise a young precocious child may fail, not from lack of conceptual thought, but from inadequate vocabulary or reading facility acquired through practice. Tests constructed to demand facility and information closely correlated with grade position effectively substitute school selection for the mental test as criterion.
requirements: Test elements must not require facility or information that younger children have not yet had the opportunity to acquire
constraints: Some confounding of age and training is acknowledged as unavoidable; the authors state the young bright may be prejudiced by absence of reading practice even in tests like opposites
target_learners: young bright children assessed before they have acquired school-taught facility
target_learning_goals: valid measurement of higher conceptual processes independent of environmental training
examples: The authors note the opposites test performance of a young precocious child may be prejudiced by inadequate vocabulary or lack of reading practice rather than lack of speed of conceptual thought

article_title: Fragmented learning from short videos modulates neural activity and connectivity during memory retrieval
citation: Wei, M., Liu, J., Wang, H., Li, Q. & Dong, G.-H. (2026). Fragmented learning from short videos modulates neural activity and connectivity during memory retrieval. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00399-y
title: Fragmented-input deficit account: short-video format disrupts information integration, cognitive control, and semantic processing during memory retrieval
description: The article's explanatory framework holds that the fragmented, fast-paced structure of short videos — not multitasking — impairs memory by disrupting three interrelated brain systems. The authors state that "learning through short videos impairs memory by disrupting brain systems involved in information integration, cognitive control, and semantic processing": reduced claustrum activation reflects difficulty reconstructing a coherent situational representation, reduced caudate activation reflects weakened top-down control, and reduced MTG activation reflects impeded deep semantic processing. Rapid context-switching may reset event boundaries, hindering integration of continuous semantic cues even in a single-viewing context.
requirements: A memory task following video exposure, with neural measures of retrieval-phase activity and connectivity
constraints: The authors state the MTG interpretation "remains a preliminary interpretation and requires further empirical validation"
fMRI does not allow direct inference of causality or temporal dynamics
the sample was drawn from a college student population, which may limit generalizability
target_learners: university students (Mage = 20.95) learning factual video content
target_learning_goals: memory formation and retrieval of factual video content
examples: Participants watched either a single continuous 10-minute clip or 7 matched short segments (30 seconds to 2.5 minutes) before an immediate four-alternative forced-choice memory test during fMRI scanning

article_title: The impact of classroom soundfield systems on reading fluency in normal-hearing students
citation: Shiels, L., Carew, P., Tomlin, D. & Rance, G. (2025). The impact of classroom soundfield systems on reading fluency in normal-hearing students. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00350-1
title: Front Row Juno sound field amplification system used in mainstream classrooms
description: The Front Row Juno is a classroom sound field amplification (SFA) system in which the teacher's voice, "recorded via a lanyard-worn microphone", is sent to loudspeakers arranged around the classroom. It elevates instructions above ambient noise and evenly distributes auditory information so the teacher need not raise their voice; typical amplification is 8–10 dB. In this study one Juno system was installed per classroom, with gain calibrated from measured teacher voice levels at six seating positions.
requirements: Classroom eligibility required an enclosed classroom with no existing SFA in use.
constraints: The study's mean 7 dB SNR improvement (from approximately −7 dB to 0 dB) fell short of the recommended +15 dB minimum for optimal learning.
target_learners: mainstream primary school students, including normal-hearing grade 3–4 children
target_learning_goals: improved access to the teacher's spoken instruction in noisy classrooms
examples: Twenty-three Victorian grade 3–4 classes each received one Front Row Juno system, alternating On and Off across three school terms.

article_title: Social interaction and conceptual change pave the way away from children’s misconceptions about the Earth
citation: Diego Pablo de la Hera, Mariano Sigman and Cecilia Ines Calero. (2019). Social interaction and conceptual change pave the way away from children 's misconceptions about the Earth. npj Science of Learning 4:12. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0051-3
title: Framework theory account of conceptual change from naive flat-earth models to a scientific spherical Earth
description: The article adopts the knowledge-as-theory / Framework Theory approach, under which children hold coherent mental models of the Earth constrained by naive presuppositions, and conceptual change proceeds "through the gradual revision of framework theories 'presuppositions". The developmental path runs from rectangular flat-earth models, through disc and dual-earth synthetic models formed "by accretion of new scientific information", to suspended-earth and finally spherical models in which people live all around a planet held by gravity. The study uses this framework to interpret peer interaction as catalyzing revision of the support presupposition, shifting children from dual to non-dual models.
requirements: Assumes children's prior conceptions form coherent theories that constrain interpretation of new information
constraints: The article notes learning pathways are complex and not linear or hierarchical
target_learners: children in early elementary school (around 7 years old, second grade)
target_learning_goals: observational astronomy and cosmology: shape of the Earth, its position in space, location of people and objects on it
examples: Dyads were paired so a less knowledgeable child interacted with a more knowledgeable peer on Earth-shape concepts, and gains clustered on the dual/not-dual axis

article_title: Neural activations associated with feedback and retrieval success
citation: Wiklund-Hörnqvist, C., Andersson, M., Jonsson, B. & Nyberg, L. (2017). Neural activations associated with feedback and retrieval success. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0013-6
title: Fronto-striatal gating account of test-enhanced learning
description: The article proposes that repeated testing with feedback strengthens memory via fronto-striatal interactions, in which "the striatum acts as a gating mechanism that regulates input of task-relevant information to the prefrontal cortex (PFC)". On this account, feedback induces updating of memory representations mediated via the striatum, and the first successful retrieval demands executive control and selective updating that become less demanding once irrelevant representations are filtered out, explaining the observed activity reduction across tests.
requirements: Feedback with the correct answer during initial testing, when knowledge level is low, to support updating of memory representations
constraints: The account is offered as a suggestion from this single fMRI study; T3 was excluded from the fMRI ANOVAs and only high-confidence 'know and correct' responses were analyzed
target_learners: young healthy adults learning foreign vocabulary
examples: Participants learned 60 Swahili–Swedish word-pairs across three consecutive cued-recall tests with feedback during event-related fMRI scanning
key_sources: Wiklund-Hörnqvist, C., Andersson, M., Jonsson, B. & Nyberg, L. (2017). Neural activations associated with feedback and retrieval success. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-017-0013-6

article_title: Frontal midline theta transcranial alternating current stimulation enhances early consolidation of episodic memory
citation: Limor Shtoots, Asher Nadler, Roni Partouche, Dorin Sharir, Aryeh Rothstein, Liran Shati & Daniel A. Levy. (2024). Frontal midline theta transcranial alternating current stimulation enhances early consolidation of episodic memory. npj Science of Learning 9:8. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00222-0
title: Frontal midline HD-tACS protocol delivering 3 Hz theta stimulation at Fz with a 4x1 ring montage
description: The stimulation apparatus is a battery-driven constant-current generator connected to a passive 4 × 1 HD-tDCS distributor delivering alternating current via five small circular electrodes in a ring montage, which "can stimulate the target region more intensively than the classical bipolar electrode montage." For the frontal theta group the central electrode was Fz, chosen for the implicated role of midline frontal theta in memory; ring electrodes were AF4, AF3, FC2, and FC1. Stimulation was 3 Hz at 1.5 mA peak-to-peak for 20 min, with 30-s ramps; sham used ramp-up/ramp-down only to preserve blinding.
requirements: Conductive gel applied under electrodes with impedance kept under 1 quality unit per electrode to maintain contact quality
constraints: Current-flow modeling estimated relatively low electric field changes (0.12 mV/mm frontal, 0.28 mV/mm parietal), lower than intensities usually required to induce neural entrainment (~0.3–0.4 mV/mm)
target_learning_goals: episodic memory for studied object pictures
examples: Electrode sites were selected using HD-Targets software, which uses a finite-element model of a template adult brain to estimate current distribution

article_title: Individual differences in frontoparietal plasticity in humans
citation: Boroshok, A. L., Park, A. T., Fotiadis, P., Velasquez, G. H., Tooley, U. A., Simon, K. R., Forde, J. C. P., Delgado Reyes, L. M., Tisdall, M. D., Bassett, D. S., Cooper, E. A. & Mackey, A. title: Open behavioral, imaging, and code release for the frontoparietal plasticity study
description: The article releases all study materials for reuse: behavioral data, task-based and control regions of interest, and values extracted from neuroimaging data are freely available on GitHub, deidentified neuroimaging data in BIDS format are on OpenNeuro, and all code used to collect task data and analyze behavioral and imaging data is on GitHub. citation: Jionghao Lin, Zifei Han, Danielle R. Thomas, Ashish Gurung, Shivang Gupta, Vincent Aleven, Kenneth R. Koedinger. (2024). How Can I Get It Right? Using GPT to Rephrase Incorrect Trainee Responses. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.00970
title: Framework for determining the quality of rephrased responses (accuracy × responsiveness)
description: A two-dimensional framework the authors propose from their evaluation results for judging the quality of rephrased feedback responses. Accuracy measures whether the rephrased response is a better example of the lesson's target practice; responsiveness measures how selectively words are changed while preserving the trainee's original words and ideas. Responses rated 1 or 2 in accuracy are acceptable; the "optimal rephrased responses should be high in both accuracy and responsiveness (i.e., Excellent area in Fig. 6)", while low-accuracy responses (≤ 0) are undesirable regardless of responsiveness.

constraints: Low responsiveness may indicate major structural and semantic changes that are harder for trainees to learn and retain, per the authors
target_learning_goals: improving quality of automated explanatory feedback
recognizing desired forms of tutoring responses
examples: A rephrasing rated accuracy 2 but responsiveness 0 (e.g., "I see you're making good progress with your efforts. Keep it up!") falls in the Good area; a human rephrasing rated accuracy -1 with high responsiveness is undesirable.

description: The survey organises the field of student free-text evaluation — the automatic evaluation of students' free-text production including short answers and essays — along two axes. After revising an earlier three-dimensional model used by Bräutigam (2014), the authors developed a heuristic competence model with "four dimensions, each divided into four sub-capabilities", covering declarative/conceptual systems knowledge, modeling systems, procedural problem solving with system models, and evaluation of models. It structures both the CK conceptualisation and the intervention content.

constraints: The model is described as heuristic; errors and insufficiencies of the earlier version were revised based on empirical study

6th-grade secondary pupils (target of systems thinking instruction)

title: Fractions Computation Test (20-item researcher-developed measure)
description: The Fractions Computation Test is a researcher-developed 20-item test (14 addition, 6 subtraction) measuring students' ability to add and subtract fractions, with "a total of 42 points on the test." Items vary by operation, denominator type (like/unlike), whether fractions appear on ruler markings, and number of stacks. Internal consistency for this sample was 0.81 at pre-test and 0.96 at post-test, and interrater agreement on a random 20% of tests was 97%. description: The article distinguishes "free active" (uncontrolled productive) vocabulary from passive vocabulary: words learners can use productively in real contexts "with minimum of thought and pauses." description: Fraction Face-Off! is a 36-lesson manualized fraction intervention for at-risk fourth graders, delivered in dyads for 12 weeks, 3 sessions per week of 35 minutes. title: Friend Supporter: a 5-week, 5-module web-based experiential learning program with role-plays, worksheets, and written psychologist feedback
description: "Friend Supporter" is a 5-week web-based experiential learning program for the adult public with no history of cancer diagnosis, centered on the scenario "What if your friend were diagnosed with cancer?" title: Frenzel's model of teacher emotion antecedents: distal classroom conditions and proximal cognitive appraisals
description: The study adopts the part of Frenzel's model dealing with antecedents of teacher emotions in classroom interactions. A key assumption is that "the cognitive appraisals of events that occur in the classroom significantly contribute to teachers' emotions", which in turn impact teaching behaviours and student outcomes. Classroom conditions reported by the whole class (discipline, situational interest) serve as distal antecedents, while teachers' control and value appraisals are proximal antecedents; the article tests whether appraisals mediate the conditions–emotions relation and asks whether the model needs adaptation for student teachers.

constraints: The article reports that for student teachers, emotions seem to be elicited by more or other variables than the model proposes, so the model may need adaptation for this group
target_learning_goals: understanding how classroom events and appraisals shape teaching-related emotions
examples: The study operationalized distal antecedents as student-reported class discipline and situational interest aggregated to lesson level, and proximal antecedents as student teachers' control and value appraisals after each of three lessons

self-control and inhibitory control in learning

A live task demonstration plus DVD reference for cognitive preparation
constraints: The cadaver model lacks bleeding, so iatrogenic bleeding control scenarios cannot be created
Cost and legal constraints make cadaveric training a precious resource limited to licensed cadaver training centers
Cadavers require up to 2 weeks of defrosting before use
target_learners: Junior surgical trainees who are novices in laparoscopic surgery
target_learning_goals: Basic laparoscopic technical skills (peg transfer, appendicectomy, knot tying) to a safe performance level
examples: Ten novices performed 10 repetitions per task on fresh frozen cadavers over 2 days, with 2.5-minute rests between repetitions and 20-minute breaks with role swaps after each task block
key_sources: Sharma Mitesh MS, Macafee David MA MD, Pranesh Nagarajan MD, Horgan Alan F. MD. (2012). Construct Validity of Fresh Frozen Human Cadaver as a Training Model in Minimal Access Surgery. JSLS : Journal of the Society of Laparoendoscopic Surgeons. https://doi.org/10.4293/108680812X13462882735818
